title: Restaurant Operations Hub
description: Dishes with food cost, inventory with par levels, suppliers, orders and shifts.
forWho: Independent restaurants and small restaurant groups

spec.useCase: Anselmo Guerrero-Whitfield owns a restaurant and uses this to see which dishes have a high food cost, what is below par and needs ordering, which orders are on the way and who is working this week.

text.text: Run the restaurant from one page: every dish with its food cost, the inventory counted against par, suppliers and their order days, purchase orders on the way, and the shifts this week. Start with the Dashboard, order whatever the Order? column flags, and review any dish marked High cost.
The vendors the restaurant orders from, with order days and lead times.
Everything counted in the walk-in and storeroom, with par levels.
Every dish with its price, plate cost and food cost percentage.
Purchase orders sent to suppliers, with expected delivery.
Who is working when, by role.
Costs, stock and supply at a glance.

cells.text: Plate cost divided by menu price
Aim for about 28 to 32 percent; over 35 means rework the plate or the price
Compares what is on hand to the par level
Order the Quantity to order, rounded to the supplier's pack size
Push dishes with a high margin and good sales
Plates sold from the point of sale report
Retire dishes that sell little and cost a lot

text.text: A plate cost is a number you keep current. Prices move; costs drift.
List every ingredient in the recipe, including oil, salt, garnish and cooking loss.
Multiply each by its cost per unit from Inventory.
Add them up; enter the total as the plate cost.
Read Food cost (%) and the Cost check.

cells.text: Keep an eye on supplier changes
Trim the portion or add a cheaper component
Raise the price or rework the dish

text.text: Recost every dish when a supplier raises a price, and at least once a quarter. Update the Last costed date.
Count at the same time each week, after close.
Count by location: walk-in, dry storage, bar, then paper goods.
Enter On hand and Last counted for each ingredient.
Look at the Order? column; anything marked Order goes on the next supplier list.
First in, first out: label dates, rotate stock.
Record waste and spills during service, not only at the count.
Set par from actual use plus a small buffer for the delivery lead time. Adjust after holidays and seasonal changes.
Open the Inventory table, read the Order? column and group the flagged items by supplier.
Create an order for each supplier with the lines and a delivery date.
Check the delivery floor on the supplier row before sending.
After the delivery, check against the invoice and press Log delivery.
Note any shortage on the order and on the supplier's notes. Three problems in a month is a reason to change suppliers.
Stations stocked and sanitizer buckets set
Stock counts updated for anything low
Equipment off, doors locked, alarm set
Small checklists done every day prevent the large problems you cannot afford.
